title: Stay Safe: Wallet Security
objectives: How to tell a phishing page from the real one before you connect
What you are actually approving when you click sign
What a delegate or an on-chain approval can do to your wallet

steps.title: The two rules that stop most attacks
steps.body:
In crypto you are the bank, which means there's no fraud department to call and no chargeback to file. Your habits are the vault.

Two rules stop most of what's out there.

**Rule one: get to the site the right way.** Phishing isn't clever code, it's a URL that looks almost right. Attackers buy the sponsored slot above search results, because that's the one link people click without reading. `phantorn.app` instead of phantom.app. `jup-airdrop.xyz` instead of the official claim page. The fix is boring and it works: bookmark the apps you use, and always reach them from the bookmark. Never from a search result, an ad, or a link in a DM.

**Rule two: believe the wallet, not the page.** When you sign, your wallet shows what will actually change - which tokens leave, what you receive. That preview is built from the transaction itself, not from the website's marketing copy. The page can say "Claim 5,000 free USDC" as loudly as it wants. If the popup shows 2.5 SOL leaving your wallet, the popup is right.

There's a third rule underneath both, and it's the one scammers actually rely on: slow down. Urgency is the business model - "claim within 10 minutes", "your wallet will be suspended". A real protocol has never once punished anyone for taking fifteen seconds to read a prompt.

steps.title: How a drainer empties a wallet
steps.body:
A drainer is rarely a hack. It's an approval you gave, waiting to be used.

Here's the usual shape. A site asks you to sign a transaction that sets *its* address as a delegate over your token accounts, or reassigns your account with a set-authority instruction. On its own it looks harmless - nothing appears to leave your wallet. Then, later, the drainer uses the permission you already granted and moves the tokens out in one transaction, without asking you again.

On Solana that happens in a single block, and a single transaction can act on several accounts at once. One careless <Term id="signature">signature</Term> can empty every token account you hold, in the same instant, with no pending state to notice and no window to react.

So the question at the signing screen isn't "does this look like a good deal?". It's "what permission am I granting, and to whom?". If a transaction asks to change an authority, add a delegate, or close an account to a destination you don't recognise, and you didn't come here to do exactly that, reject it.

questions.prompt: You see a sponsored Google result for a popular exchange offering a 'bonus $500 reward'. What is the safest action?
options: Click the ad immediately to claim the bonus
Ignore the ad and reach the site from a bookmark you saved yourself
Connect a wallet that holds your main savings
Approve whatever the page asks without reading it
questions.explainRight: Ignore the ad. Ad slots are cheap to buy and easy to point at a lookalike domain - the real site comes from your own bookmark.
questions.explainWrong: Never open a crypto app through a sponsored ad. Lookalike domains sit at the top of search results on purpose.

questions.prompt: Your wallet popup says it is sending 5 SOL to an unknown address, but the webpage says you are claiming an airdrop. What do you do?
options: Approve it anyway, the page knows what it is doing
Wait five minutes and approve it then
Refresh the browser and approve it again
questions.explainRight: Reject it. The popup describes the transaction you are actually authorising - it is the only version that matters.
questions.explainWrong: Reject. The popup shows the real on-chain instruction. The webpage is telling you a story.
